svg.aria-label: System.nanoTime is the only correct deadline basis. Left, a wall-clock deadline built from System.currentTimeMillis: start plus the watchlist provider's 30 second timeout gives deadline 1,030,000; an NTP step moves the clock backward by one hour, and the loop check currentTimeMillis less than deadline stays true, so the timeout fires about an hour late, or immediately if the step is forward instead. Right, a monotonic deadline built from System.nanoTime: deadline is start plus 30,000,000,000 nanoseconds, and the loop checks nanoTime minus deadline less than zero, which is immune to clock steps and wraps correctly through Long overflow; the broken alternative nanoTime greater than or equal to deadline compares an arbitrary per-JVM origin directly and can be false forever or true immediately near overflow.
svg.text: System.nanoTime() IS THE ONLY CORRECT DEADLINE BASIS
WALL-CLOCK DEADLINE — currentTimeMillis()
MONOTONIC DEADLINE — nanoTime()
start = System.currentTimeMillis()
= 1,000,000 (ms since epoch)
deadline = start + 30_000
= 1,030,000 (watchlist-provider 30 s timeout)
NTP steps the wall clock backward
clock jumps by -3,600,000 ms (1 hour)
(a forward step is the same failure, opposite direction)
while (currentTimeMillis() < deadline) park(...)
loop re-reads the wall clock every iteration
TIMEOUT FIRES ~1 HOUR LATE
now stays below 1,030,000 for about an hour
after the real 30 s already elapsed
(forward step instead: timeout fires immediately)
WHY
currentTimeMillis() is wall-clock time. NTP sync,
leap-second slew, and manual changes can move it —
backward as well as forward — at any moment, so a
deadline computed from it is not trustworthy.
start = System.nanoTime()
= t0 (arbitrary per-JVM origin, not epoch time)
deadline = start + 30_000_000_000L
30 s expressed in nanoseconds
while (nanoTime() - deadline < 0) park(...)
subtraction form — monotonic, immune to NTP steps
wraps correctly even across Long overflow of nanoTime()
BROKEN: nanoTime() >= deadline
direct comparison — nanoTime()'s origin is arbitrary
near Long overflow this is false forever, or true at once
WHY THE SUBTRACTION FORM WINS
nanoTime() only promises differences between two calls
are meaningful. (a - b) >= 0 relies on two's-complement
wraparound to stay correct past Long.MAX_VALUE; a
direct >= comparison has no such guarantee.
computed value (start / deadline)
loop / check step
correct — safe deadline form
broken — clock step or bad comparison
A → B : B happens after A, in program order
annotation panel — explains the "why"
